query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a thin, conformal metal layer that acts as a wetting agent (e.g., via atomic layer deposition of nickel) prior to spark‐plasma sintering will improve copper infiltration and interfacial bonding. This intervention should yield a more uniform composite microstructure with fewer voids compared to vapor-coated W powders, while retaining the necessary mechanical durability for fusion-reactor joint applications.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix produced via conventional vapor-coating sintering methods that display incomplete wetting, void formation, and phase separation.
generation.intervention: Apply an atomic layer deposition (ALD) of a thin Ni coating over tungsten particles before consolidation using spark‐plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: Processing under high vacuum with controlled temperature ramping typical of spark‐plasma sintering; service conditions include high heat flux and irradiation environments representative of fusion-reactor joints.
generation.structural_mediator: The thin Ni layer promotes improved wettability between tungsten and copper by reducing the surface energy mismatch at the interface, thus enabling near-perfect contact during rapid sintering.
generation.mechanism: The Ni coating enhances the interfacial adhesion and capillary infiltration of molten Cu during sintering, reducing void nucleation and phase separation. This increased interfacial quality is expected to facilitate better thermal transport while maintaining mechanical strength under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline vapor-coated W powders, the Ni-coated W composite will show a more uniform microstructure with fewer voids. Improved thermal conductivity and sustained mechanical durability under simulated fusion-relevant irradiation are anticipated.
generation.baseline: Vapor-coated W powders sintered to achieve near-perfect constituent contact but which may still exhibit voids and phase separation.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the Ni interlayer is expected to hold under the sintering temperatures and microstructural regimes typical for spark‐plasma sintering; however, its performance under extreme irradiation doses or at higher-than-standard processing temperatures remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in thermal conductivity and long-term irradiation stability is uncertain until experimentally measured. Additionally, potential effects of the Ni layer on other properties (e.g., corrosion resistance) under fusion reactor conditions require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of composites: one set using tungsten particles pre-coated with a thin Ni layer (via ALD) and a control set using the standard vapor-coating method. Subject both sets to spark‐plasma sintering under identical processing conditions and then expose them to simulated fusion-reactor thermal and irradiation conditions.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM/TEM) to quantify void fraction and interface quality
Thermal conductivity tests across typical operating temperatures
Mechanical durability and strength tests before and after irradiation exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated W composites do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in void fraction, improved thermal transport, and maintained mechanical strength relative to the baseline, then the proposed hypothesis is refuted.
